title: AI Sales Roleplay in 30+ Languages: How to Train Reps for Every Market
summary: How to run AI sales roleplay in 30+ languages: localize the buyer, keep one scorecard across markets, review calls you can't speak, and pilot by region.
body_markdown:
Roleplay


On this page


Multilingual AI sales roleplay lets reps practice with an AI buyer who speaks the language of the market they sell into, then scores each call against the same criteria the home team uses. Quotain's AI buyers speak 30+ languages, including German, Japanese, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Korean, Chinese and Arabic, and the accent can be set for each buyer. The approach that works is simple: localize the buyer, keep the scorecard fixed, and have someone who knows the market review the scenario before reps practice.


## TL;DR


- Localize the buyer for each market: call language, accent, company, buying context and the objections that market raises.
- Keep one scorecard across markets, so a rep in Munich and a rep in Monterrey are graded on the same behaviors.
- Managers can review calls in languages they don't speak: Quotain writes coaching in the reviewer's interface language and keeps quotes and suggested lines in the call language.
- Pilot one scenario in two regions, check the scores with an in-market reviewer, then expand.


## Why reps should practice in the buyer's language


A rep who handles a price objection well in English can still stall when the same objection arrives in German or Japanese. The words change, and so do the approval habits behind them. A procurement lead in Munich may need EU data processing before a deal can move. A buyer in Tokyo may need local reference customers to get a proposal through internal approval. A buyer in Monterrey may not get a proposal priced in dollars approved at all.


If reps only practice in English, they meet these moments for the first time on a live call with a deal at stake. Practice in the call language moves that first attempt into a session where a mistake costs nothing and the rep can retry the exact line.


## What to localize and what to keep the same


### Localize the buyer


- Call language and accent. In Quotain, the accent is set for each buyer or chosen automatically from the company and buyer context. The accents available vary by language.
- Role, company and buying context. A head of purchasing at a logistics firm in Germany buys differently from a VP of sales at a US startup.
- Local objections. Data residency, currency, local references, approval steps and procurement rules are the usual places a market differs.
- Tone and pace. How formal the buyer is, and how directly they say no, should match what your in-market team hears.


### Keep the standard fixed


Attach the same scorecard to every market's simulation. Criteria such as "anchored value before price," "tied price to business impact" and "secured a dated next step" read the same in any language. When the criteria stay fixed, a gap between two regions points to a coaching need you can act on. Add a market-specific line only when a market truly requires an extra step, such as answering a data residency question before price.


## How managers review calls in a language they don't speak


Quotain writes coaching feedback in the reviewer's interface language and keeps transcript quotes and suggested words in the language of the call, so the evidence is never paraphrased. A sales leader in New York can read why a Japanese renewal call missed "anchored value before price," jump to the line at its timestamp, and see the suggested next line in Japanese for the rep.


The Quotain interface (menus, emails, scorecards and coaching text) is also available in 30+ languages, in beta. The language the AI buyer speaks on a call is a separate setting. During a pilot, ask a native speaker or in-market manager to score a sample of calls by hand and compare their scores with the AI's, so you know the scoring reads tone and phrasing the way a local buyer would.


## A two-region pilot you can run in two weeks


1. Pick one conversation that matters in both markets, such as a renewal pricing review or a first discovery call.
2. Build the buyer once, then make a version for each market with the local language, accent, company and objections.
3. Attach one scorecard to both versions.
4. Have each rep run at least two attempts, and retry the moment the scorecard flags.
5. Ask an in-market reviewer to score a sample by hand and compare those scores with the AI scores.
6. Compare the two regions on the same criteria, choose one behavior to coach in each, and run the scenario again a week later.


If the reviewer agrees with the scores and reps improve on the retry, add the next market. If the reviewer disagrees, fix the buyer or the criteria before you scale.

## Frequently asked questions


### Which AI sales roleplay tools train reps in many languages?


Several vendors list multilingual practice, and the language lists change often, so check each vendor's current page and run a real call in every language you need. Quotain's AI buyers speak 30+ languages on every plan, with accents set for each buyer.


### Can reps practice with local accents?


Yes. In Quotain, you set the accent for each buyer, or let Quotain choose it from the company and buyer context. The accents available vary by language, so test the ones your reps will hear.


### Should every market use the same sales scorecard?


Use the same core criteria everywhere so you can compare regions fairly. Add a market-specific line only when that market requires a step the others don't, such as a data residency answer or a local reference.


### Can a manager coach a call in a language they don't speak?


Yes. Quotain writes the coaching in the manager's interface language and keeps the quotes and suggested words in the call language. Have an in-market reviewer spot-check scores during the pilot.


### Which sales readiness tools support reps who sell in multiple languages?


Look for three things: practice calls in each language your reps sell in, one scorecard that applies across languages, and review tools that let a manager read feedback in their own language. Quotain covers all three, with AI buyers in 30+ languages and an interface in 30+ languages, in beta.
